content: Dr. Xavier Bosch-Capblanch, a group leader at the Swiss Tropical and Public Health Institute (Swiss TPH), is the primary contact for this work. Meike Zuske from Swiss TPH coordinated the contributors. The reviewers included Ekpereonne Esu and Chioma Moses Oringanje from the University of Calabar, who focused on effectiveness and safety reviews, and Heather Ames from Swiss TPH, who conducted a feasibility scoping review. Peter Steinmann, an expert in lymphatic filariasis, and Amanda Ross, a statistical analyst from Swiss TPH, also contributed. John Eyers from Swiss TPH served as the search strategist. Acknowledgments are extended to Jonathan King from the World Health Organization (WHO) for coordinating the review with WHO guidelines, facilitating discussions among various groups, and providing guidance. Mohammed T. Ansari reviewed the GRADE evidence profiles. Special thanks are given to Gary Weil, Joshua Bogus, and Charles Goss from Washington University in St. Louis for sharing data from ongoing studies and responding to requests. The global elimination of lymphatic filariasis (LF) as a public health problem was targeted for 2020. However, as of now, 29 out of 55 countries requiring mass drug administration (MDA) are not on track to meet this goal. Some countries are only beginning to scale up MDA efforts, which require a minimum of five years to implement effectively. Many governments and donors have committed resources only through 2020, and further commitments are uncertain. Countries initiating MDA are seeking advice from WHO on alternative strategies to accelerate progress and potentially stop MDA by the target elimination date. Additionally, countries already on track are requesting guidance on addressing suboptimal responses to current MDA strategies, such as districts with persistent infection rates despite multiple MDA rounds, failed transmission assessment surveys (TAS), and hotspots of infection identified during post-MDA surveillance. WHO is expected to recommend strategies to overcome these challenges and must respond promptly to national program queries by grading available evidence and establishing recommendations that consider the accessibility and feasibility of alternative strategies. Alternative MDA strategies, such as twice-yearly MDA with ivermectin, have been identified as potentially more effective in reducing infection below elimination thresholds in less time. Mathematical models support this approach, and pharmacokinetic studies of a three-drug combination (ivermectin, diethylcarbamazine citrate, and albendazole) have shown superior parasite-killing effects without increased serious adverse events in individuals with heavy parasite loads. This strategy could potentially lead to permanent sterilization or destruction of adult worms, reducing infection and transmission in endemic communities more effectively than current strategies. Randomized clinical studies of the three-drug strategy for community-wide treatment have been initiated in five countries, with safety data available for meta-analysis. However, the use of diethylcarbamazine in countries co-endemic with onchocerciasis and/or loiasis is not recommended. In such settings, twice-yearly treatment with the current two-drug regimen may serve as an alternative approach. To provide the WHO guideline development group with the best available evidence, the Swiss TPH conducted an updated systematic review (SR) on mass chemotherapy for LF. This report includes the methods and results of the SR on effectiveness and safety, as well as a feasibility scoping review of qualitative evidence on community perceptions of MDA regimens. The systematic review on effectiveness and safety aimed to identify alternative MDA strategies that are more effective and as safe as the current strategy for LF elimination. The review included randomized and cohort studies, as well as comparative studies with individualor community-level allocation of interventions. Participants included individuals infected with or communities endemic for Wuchereria bancrofti or Brugia species. Interventions and comparisons included various MDA regimens, such as annual or biannual administration of ivermectin, diethylcarbamazine, and albendazole, depending on the co-endemicity of onchocerciasis or loiasis. Effectiveness outcomes included microfilaria clearance, microfilaria density, circulating filarial antigen levels, IgG4 response to Brugia Rapid or PanLF, and other markers of LF infection. Safety outcomes included the frequency and severity of adverse events, classified into grades ranging from mild to life-threatening or fatal. Data sources included published, unpublished, and ongoing studies, with individual-level safety data provided by Washington University in St. Louis. The risk of bias (ROB) in included studies was assessed using standard methods, considering factors such as sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, and reporting completeness. The quality of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach, which considers study design, ROB, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and other factors. For binary outcomes, effect estimates were expressed as relative risks (RR) of the intervention compared to the control group. Meta-analyses were conducted when multiple studies reported on the same comparison, outcome, and follow-up duration. Heterogeneity was assessed using the I² statistic, and random-effects models were consistently used for pooled estimates. The qualitative scoping review aimed to synthesize community and drug distributor perceptions and experiences of MDA campaigns for LF elimination. This included studies from countries undertaking MDA campaigns, focusing on themes such as community acceptance, challenges, and the role of drug distributors. Mixed-methods studies were included if qualitative findings could be extracted. This comprehensive review provides critical insights into the effectiveness, safety, and community perceptions of MDA strategies, informing WHO recommendations for LF elimination.
